item.title: AI Literacy at Work: Implications for Human Resource Management
item.content:encoded:
Maarten Renkema, University of Twente

Laura Lamers, University of Twente

Christoph Lutz, BI Norwegian Business School

Anna B. Holm, Aarhus University

Organizations are rapidly adopting AI technologies, but this creates significant challenges including algorithmic bias and opacity. AI literacy—the knowledge, skills, and attitudes enabling individuals to engage effectively and critically with AI—has become essential for competitive survival and is now mandated by the EU's AI Act. However, research on AI literacy remains focused primarily on educational contexts and individual learners, leaving organizational and HRM perspectives largely unexplored.

This special issue seeks to advance theoretical understanding of AI literacy as an organizational phenomenon rather than merely an individual competency. The editors invite contributions that move beyond both naive enthusiasm and dismissive skepticism, instead adopting critically engaged perspectives grounded in empirical evidence. Contributions should examine AI literacy across multiple organizational levels—individual, team, and organizational—and explore how HRM can facilitate its development and implications for HR functions and practices.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Implications of AI literacy for core HRM functions including recruitment, selection, learning and development, performance management, and employee well-being
  • Organizational AI literacy: design, implementation, and governance of HRM activities
  • Emergence mechanisms through which individual AI literacy becomes collective organizational capability
  • Relationship between organizational AI literacy and adjacent constructs such as organizational AI readiness
  • Competition for AI talent and inequality implications
  • Team design and composition to enable and develop AI literacy
  • HRM and HRD practices supporting AI-literate teams including workforce planning, staffing, job design, and training
  • Levels and combinations of AI literacy needed across different teams and roles
  • Manifestation of AI literacy in everyday work practices
  • Technical, ethical and practical dimensions of AI literacy in AI-mediated recruitment
  • AI literacy's influence on employees' AI overreliance and fairness perceptions
  • AI literacy of HR professionals and its influence on adoption of AI tools

item.title: Addressing Ultra-Low Fertility and Workforce Shrinkage: A Human-Centered HRM Response to the Demographic Crisis
item.content:encoded:
Ingyu Oh, Kansai Gaidai University

Jie Wu, University of Aberdeen

Ho Kwong Kwan, China Europe International Business School

Hyun Jeong Kim, Inha University

Ultra-low fertility is reshaping human resource management across East Asia, Europe, and North America, making workforce planning and retention strategic imperatives. Organizations are adopting innovative HRM practices including work-life balance initiatives, inclusive hiring, and technology-enabled solutions to address demographic decline and workforce shrinkage.

The special issue welcomes rigorous theoretical and empirical research on human-centered strategies that balance organizational sustainability with employee wellbeing. Comparative, cross-national studies accounting for contextual differences in how fertility challenges manifest are particularly encouraged. Submissions should engage with existing HRM theories or propose new frameworks explaining the relationship between fertility patterns, cultural norms, and organizational practices.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Beyond AI: HRM and the Work of the Future
item.content:encoded:
Sandra Fisher, FH Münster

Janet Marler, University at Albany - SUNY

Guido Hertel, University of Münster

This special issue examines how artificial intelligence and related technologies reshape human resource management practices and organizational work. Building on decades of e-HRM research, the collection investigates AI's transformative potential while remaining critical of its limitations, including bias, lack of transparency, and skill erosion concerns.

The issue welcomes research exploring which HRM processes should be automated versus augmented, what alternative technologies might complement or replace AI, and what comes after the current wave of AI advancement. It seeks evidence-based scholarship that helps organizations implement AI to benefit all stakeholders while avoiding technological determinism.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Digital Nomadism and the Future of HRM: Rethinking Work, Workforce, and Workplace
item.content:encoded:
Matej Černe, University of Ljubljana

Marko Orel, Prague University of Economics and Business

Fabiola Mancinelli, University of Barcelona

Stefanie Reissner, Durham University

Brian Harney, Dublin City University

Digital nomadism represents location-independent work performed with geographic mobility, raising significant questions for human resource management regarding how organizations manage workers with fluid employment relationships and changing work locations. This special issue seeks scholarship that examines digital nomadism as both a distinctive research context and a lens for reconsidering fundamental HRM concepts in the context of distributed, fragmented, and fluid work arrangements.

The issue addresses a gap in HRM research by bringing together topics often studied separately—remote work, global mobility, platform work, and transnational employment regulation. Contributors are encouraged to develop theory-driven research that demonstrates implications for HRM phenomena, systems, and practices, moving beyond descriptive accounts of digital nomads as a lifestyle group to examine organizational and institutional dimensions.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Work design, job demands and resources, autonomy, flexibility, isolation, insecurity, time-zone dispersion, infrastructure variability, and performance
  • Leadership, coordination, voice, psychological safety, performance management, and feedback in mobile and distributed work arrangements
  • The implications of digitalization, AI, algorithmic management, and digital platforms for where, how, and under what contractual conditions work is performed
  • Talent attraction, selection, retention, and employer branding for mobile and location-independent workers
  • Careers, employability, career self-management, protean careers, sustainable careers, and boundaryless or globally mobile talent pathways
  • Wellbeing, recovery, work-nonwork boundaries, social embeddedness, loneliness, identity, and community among digital nomads and other mobile workers
  • Onboarding, socialization, belonging, organizational identification, informal learning, and knowledge sharing when workers are geographically mobile
  • Destination ecosystems, coworking spaces, local communities, employers, governments, and intermediaries as actors shaping mobile digital work
  • Comparative research on digital nomadism across countries, regions, sectors, occupations, employment forms, and regulatory regimes
  • Employment relationships, psychological contracts, commitment, fairness, inclusion, and duty of care in remote, freelance, contractual, hybrid, or employee-based arrangements
  • International HRM, global mobility, digital nomad visas, taxation, labor law, social security, cross-border compliance, data protection, and institutional complexity
  • HR architecture and governance: balancing flexibility, autonomy, coordination, control, equity, risk management, and organizational support

Timeline

  • April 30, 2027: Manuscript deadline

item.title: The Institutional Fragility of Inclusion in Contemporary HRM Systems
item.content:encoded:
Benjamin Laker, Henley Business School, University of Reading

Sven Horak, St. John's University

Toyin Ajibade Adisa, Royal Docks School of Business and Law, University of East London

Fulya Acikgoz, University of Sussex Business School

This special issue investigates how inclusion in human resource management has become institutionally fragile—endorsed in principle but inconsistently enacted or maintained symbolically without substantive commitment. It examines how identity is constructed, contested, and regulated through HRM practices when political, economic, organisational, and cultural pressures destabilise the systems that once supported inclusion.

The issue seeks theoretical, empirical, and methodological contributions that conceptualise inclusion as a dynamic process shaped by power, legitimacy, and resistance. Submissions should examine how HRM practices reinforce dominant norms, marginalise difference, or become sites of identity contestation. Contributions drawing on intersectionality, social identity theory, critical race theory, feminism, or postcolonial perspectives are particularly welcome, as are comparative studies exploring how inclusion operates across different institutional and cultural contexts.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Institutional fragility of inclusion
  • Identity construction and negotiation in HRM
  • Symbolic inclusion versus substantive change
  • Performance systems and cultural fit criteria
  • Comparative and global inclusion analyses
  • HRM as voice suppression and identity masking
  • Intersectional identity effects on opportunity and recognition
  • Informal networks and shadow structures in inclusion
  • Organisational responses to erosion of inclusion mandates
  • Institutional logics and politics of belonging
  • Decolonial and Indigenous critiques of inclusion frameworks

Timeline

  • December 15, 2026: Manuscript deadline

item.title: The Interplay of Human Resource Management and Leadership: Alignment, Tensions, and Consequences
item.content:encoded:
Aneeqa Suhail, Tilburg University

Steven Kilroy, Trinity College Dublin

Robin Bauwens, Tilburg University

Sut I Wong, BI Norwegian Business School

Sasa Batistič, Tilburg University

This special issue examines the dynamic relationship between human resource management systems and leadership behaviors, addressing how they align, conflict, or substitute for one another in shaping organizational outcomes. The issue recognizes that while HRM and leadership research have traditionally developed as separate streams, they operate interdependently in practice. Understanding their interplay is essential for comprehending how people management actually functions in organizations and for developing more effective, coherent approaches to managing employees.

Appel publié par The International Journal of Human Resource Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How HRM systems and leadership behaviors interact in shaping employee and organizational outcomes across organizational levels
  • Different forms of alignment between HRM and leadership (supplementary fit, complementary fit, perceptual filtering) and their distinct consequences
  • When and how HRM systems function as substitutes for leadership and resulting consequences
  • How misalignment between HRM systems and leadership behaviors emerges, persists, or becomes institutionalized
  • When alignment amplifies negative outcomes such as work intensification, role overload, or employee strain
  • How employees interpret and respond to misalignment or substitution between HRM systems and leadership
  • Which configurations of HRM systems and leadership strengthen effectiveness of remote and hybrid work arrangements
  • How leaders enact, adapt, or resist HRM systems when leading employees at a distance
  • Employee experiences of alignment and misalignment in remote and hybrid work settings
  • How HRM-leadership configurations evolve over time and affect employee and organizational outcomes
  • How temporal shifts in leadership behaviors or HRM systems alter the balance between substitution and complementarity

Timeline

  • March 31, 2027: Full paper submission deadline
